title: Thomas (3 July)
hookLine: the doubter who, tradition says, took the gospel to India

lines: THE MAN WHO OFFERED TO DIE.
cards: "Doubting Thomas." People say it at work about the colleague who wants to see the numbers, and at home about the kid who won't believe the stove is hot. It has stuck to him.

But in John's Gospel, the first time we hear this man speak, he offers to die. And when he finally believes, what he says about Jesus is startlingly plain. Today, a witness with a nickname he might not have chosen.

teach.h: LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE.
teach.b: First scene. Jesus decides to go back toward Judea, where people had tried to stone him, because his friend Lazarus has died. The disciples protest.
Thomas, John says, "who is called Didymus," Greek for twin, turns to the others: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Grim, maybe. But brave.
Second scene. On the evening of the resurrection day, Jesus appears to the disciples, and Thomas isn't there. They tell him.
He refuses to take it secondhand.

teach.h: UNLESS I SEE, I WILL NOT BELIEVE.
teach.b: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's the line that earned the nickname.
Third scene, eight days later. Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, stands among them, and offers Thomas exactly what he asked for: put your finger here, see my hands.
John never says Thomas touches him. What he says is: "Thomas answered, and said to him: My Lord and my God." Not teacher.
Not prophet. Catholics hear in it a full confession of faith in Jesus, from the man who wouldn't believe secondhand. Jesus answers: blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.
Then the Gospel goes quiet about him. Tradition carries on.
It says Thomas went east, preached in India, and died there as a martyr.
Some Christians in India, above all the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, trace their church to him. Historians debate the details. For those churches, the tradition is their own story.

how: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle on 3 July; in India, the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala keep it as the feast of the apostle they trace their church to.

o: the apostle called the Twin, who said my Lord and my God
the apostle who first carried the gospel to Rome
the disciple who betrayed Jesus for thirty silver coins

p: let us also go, that we may die with him

s: John says Thomas put his finger in the wounds
Jesus offers, but John never says he touched; he records only Thomas's answer.
Thomas once offered to go and die with Jesus
before Lazarus is raised: let us also go, that we may die with him.
Thomas's story ends in the Gospels
the Gospels go quiet, but tradition says he preached and died in India.

games.q: you're Thomas. the others say they've seen the risen Lord. you weren't there. what do you do?
o: say you won't believe unless you see the wounds.
games.why: Thomas refused to take it secondhand, and eight days later Jesus came back and offered him exactly that.

practice: Bring to mind the churches of India, old communities and new, in cities and villages, some small and under pressure, and picture a family going to church on a hot morning, in a language you may not know.
If you pray, say Thomas's words slowly, once, my Lord and my God, and offer them for those communities. If you don't, simply wish them peace and safety.

wordCard.voice: Thomas. The apostle called the Twin, who doubted, then said my Lord and my God, and who, tradition says, carried the gospel to India.

orig.note: Greek: twin — John's name for Thomas.

carryVoice: Your line: my lord and my god. The plainest words came from the one who asked to see. See you tomorrow.
